extracted.intended_audience: researchers, policymakers, UNDP staff, and media professionals studying or concerned with media coverage of climate change and its policy/aid implications
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and researching how mass media report on climate change (including mitigation and adaptation), the journalistic norms that shape coverage, and the influence of that coverage on public opinion and foreign aid mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of how much media attention climate change (and adaptation) receives over time (e.g., counts of newspaper articles and TV segments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper presents multiple figures and tables tracking increases in quantity of coverage over years and months across many newspapers and television programs — use article/segment counts and time-series to assess attention levels and trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty as a journalistic norm
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic preference for novelty shapes what gets reported; novelty is listed as a key input in journalistic norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether stories emphasize new or sensational elements; novelty interacts with other norms (e.g., balance) to influence story selection and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance (and 'bias as balance')
rubrics_metrics.description: The journalistic norm of 'balance' — often invoked to present opposing views — which can produce biased representations of scientific consensus (see 'bias as balance').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether coverage presents manufactured balance by giving disproportionate weight to minority skeptical voices; review Boykoff & Boykoff (2004) examples where balance created misleading impressions of scientific debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency in news production to personalize climate change stories (focus on individuals/characters rather than broader processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess stories for individual-focused narratives that may downplay structural, systemic, or scientific complexity; personalization is listed among interacting journalistic norms and outputs (e.g., drama-tization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on dramatic elements in reporting (spectacle, dramatic rescues, striking visuals) that shape public perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine use of dramatic imagery and storytelling (e.g., televised rescues in the Mozambique floods) and its role in garnering audience attention and mobilizing aid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority–Order (source selection / who is cited)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which actors are cited as legitimate sources in stories — scientific experts, politicians, NGOs, military — shaping the story's authority and framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate source selection and whether coverage privileges certain authorities over others; the paper asks 'who gets cited as legitimate sources' as a central question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue Attention Cycle / competition for public attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Climate stories compete with immediate local issues for attention; issue rises and falls (Downs' Issue Attention Cycle) affecting marginality in national budgets and policymaker focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze timing and persistence of coverage relative to other news issues; consider how competition for attention leads to episodic rather than sustained coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of scientific uncertainty and scepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: How media represent uncertainty in climate science and the presence/influence of climate 'sceptics' that can paralyze action or create public confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect whether uncertainty is contextualized appropriately; note examples where sceptic voices demobilize action versus cases of clearer scientific reporting (see Boykoff & Boykoff 2004, 2007).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage balance between mitigation and adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which media cover climate change mitigation (reducing emissions) versus adaptation (responses to impacts), with adaptation coverage noted as under-researched and emerging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure topic emphasis in stories — technical mitigation topics (e.g., carbon sequestration) versus biological/human processes and adaptation — and identify gaps where adaptation is insufficiently covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of moral, ethical and cultural issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reporting addresses the moral, ethical and cultural dimensions of climate change, not just technical aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence and depth of discussion on inequality, justice, and cultural impacts (paper notes coverage has found moral/ethical/cultural issues ‘more difficult to effectively cover’).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural economic and political pressures on media
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that commercial media depend on advertising (from industries tied to consumption), which constrains willingness to repeatedly call for revolutionary societal changes needed for serious mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional constraints (ownership, revenue sources, advertiser influence) that shape editorial choices and limit certain narratives (e.g., anti-consumption messages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Media's ability to mobilize humanitarian aid
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which media images and reporting generate international assistance and donor responses (e.g., Mozambique floods received far greater TV coverage and aid compared to other disasters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case studies and comparative coverage-to-aid analyses (e.g., televised images leading to greater humanitarian assistance) to assess causal links between media coverage and aid flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter access, immediacy and completeness of coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Level of media access to disaster zones and immediacy of reporting (e.g., reporters' near-immediate access in Mozambique enabled spectacular coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess constraints on journalist access and how presence/absence in the field affects the amount and nature of coverage, including visual/spectacular content that drives attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public engagement outcomes (knowledge, trust, emotions, mobilization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of how media coverage affects public knowledge, feelings (isolation, hopelessness, powerlessness), trust in government, and propensity to take action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate surveys and studies of citizen knowledge and engagement; the paper highlights demobilizing effects of certain coverage patterns and the influential role of media in forming public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative and geographic breadth of coverage studies
rubrics_metrics.description: The need to examine media coverage across a wider range of countries (beyond US/UK) — e.g., China, India, Brazil — to clarify impediments and enhance action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing media coverage, include cross-national comparisons and analyses of key players in international climate negotiations; the paper calls for more research in diverse national contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical methods for linking coverage to policy and aid outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaches and evidence (e.g., comparative case studies, time-series analyses) to test how reporting on disasters drives aid agency budgeting and policy responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mixed methods (statistical analyses of coverage vs aid, case studies like Mozambique, and content analysis) to substantiate claims about media influence on budgets and policy decisions.
